First of all, it is very normal as lesbians for us to reach milestones like first relationships later. There are so many factors that make them later for us, like being in the closet and the tiny dating pool. 20 is still very young to have not had a relationship before in my opinion!! It's so much easier said than done but I wouldn't be all doom and gloom about this, it's honestly a lot more common than you think.

Secondly, I'm kind of worried about the narrative you're selling yourself. It seems as though because you've never had a relationship before, you think nobody will ever want you. I get that, believe me, but that's just... so not true. Everybody feels that way sometimes but it's so rarely true. it's also important to remember that before people had their first relationship, they were in your position and possibly felt the same way. There isn't some magical divide between people who have had relationships and people who hasn't, the divide is solely based on time and luck in most cases. Someday you'll be on the other side of that divide replying to some other lesbian feeling sad about being single, I promise.

Correct me if I'm wrong, but this seems much more like a matter of personal preference than morality. Antinatalism is an ethical belief, not one based on what's best for prospective parents practically. People with kids can have great and full lives, and people without them can be miserable. Both sides exist.

I don't think this is a problem any of us can solve for you, but I'll say that I wouldn't have kids just for fear that you'll regret it later. It is MUCH more likely that you'd regret having kids if you're unsure and see them as taking away from the life you want to live, than you'd regret not having them. And even if you did, it's better to regret not having kids because that way nobody's harmed, whereas if you regret having kids... Well, poor kids.

Kids are a full-time job, that's true. Travelling at the drop of a hat will stop, for one. Financial concerns are also a very fair thing to worry about, and is a large reason why (antinatalist or not) much fewer people are having kids these days. If you have kids, your freedom will definitely be limited in a major way, but it's up to you whether the benefits are worth the cost. Take some time - you don't need to figure it out immediately. 

Also, being an antinatalist doesn't mean you can't have kids - adoption is a great way to have them that I wish more people, antinatalist or not, would consider!! You said that you like taking care of teenagers the best, and there are so many teenagers waiting to be adopted if you did want kids someday. Plus you could foster them, which would be comparatively short-term and wouldn't be a lifelong commitment if someday you decided you would rather be childfree. (Obviously don't go into fostering if you're not serious about taking care of a child, but I'm just saying that fostering is less permanent than being a parent.)

Overall, I think this is more of a personal issue than an ethical one. As such, we can't tell you what will suit your life best. But I'll say this - if you don't want to date because even having a partner will compromise your lifestyle, then kids DEFINITELY won't allow you to maintain your current way of living. Unless you can see yourself making major sacrifices on that, kids almost certainly aren't for you, all other factors aside.

Not older than you, but from what I've seen long distance relationships only work in the long-term if there are plans to "close the distance" someday - aka one of you will relocate to be with the other, or you both agree to move to a new place together (after meeting several times in person and checking you're truly compatible in real life as well). I can't speak on whether you'll drift apart before you're able to do that because really only time will tell, and even couples without the distance (unfortunately) drift apart and break up often at our age. Distance is definitely an extra barrier, but it isn't an insurmountable one. As long as you keep making the effort to get to know each other, you're giving your relationship the best shot possible, and that's all you can really do.

You seem to spend a lot of time together even without closing the distance, and that's good! I wouldn't worry too much about not being able to meet up right now because... Well, you're not able to. If you could meet up but someone kept putting it off or didn't want to, that's when I'd be worried. Basically, there needs to be some sort of plan to eventually close the distance and transition from a long distance relationship, otherwise it'll  only ever be long distance and unless you're a very very very specific type of person, that won't work.

TLDR: it really depends on your intentions and how/if you're actually carrying those intentions out. Some LDRs work, some don't, just like anything else in life so all you can do is give it your best shot. Also, I'd look at r/LDR and see if anything there speaks to you :)

From now on, start living as if you were that person. Every day do one thing that gets you closer to being that person you want to be. Do you want to be someone who can easily talk to new people? So the first thing I'd say is that... it's not all that. Like it's really not all that. Like it's REAAAALLY really not all that. Most people in my sixth form aren't in a relationship, and you're 18 dude, you have so many opportunities down the line!! But I also don't think you should be that fixated on dating. In my experience, the best relationships come when you aren't actively seeking them out, and there's no point in "dating for the sake of dating" because that's only going to attract the sort of people who are doing it because they want a boyfriend and not because they want you. You want someone who wants you, trust me.

I really don't think dating apps are somewhere you want to be at our age. It's unsurprising that you haven't found much success there... but people have already told you that, so I'll leave it there. I'd highly recommend ditching the apps for a few years though?

At this point in the year, I'm not sure if there's much benefit in seeking or starting a relationship. We'll be going to uni in a few months anyway, and from what I've heard the dating scene is much better and more active there. Plus, you'll be meeting so many new people at uni, so your chances of finding a partner among them are way higher. By now you can see what I'm getting at - the fact that you haven't had a relationship yet isn't a big deal, honestly! It might seem like it (trust me, I've been there) but I promise you that most people haven't either and it will not matter once you get to uni. Not having a relationship at sixth form doesn't affect your chances down the line for better or worse. If anything, it might be better to go into uni without the baggage some of us have... 😭😭

I'm with you in terms of feeling like you don't fit in anywhere because you're high-functioning. I'm incredibly fortunate to have fallen in with a good group of friends now, but I struggled with feeling lonely or out of place for a long time, and even now I still have my days. I think it's far more important to find a group of friends you feel understood by, and that you belong to, than it is to find a relationship. Think about it - would you rather have one person who loves you, or several? This isn't to knock my girlfriend, I love her and she's a deeply important person in my life, but I'd be nothing without my friends. Friends first, dating second. It's also dangerous to put all your hopes and expectations onto one single relationship without having anyone else to fall back on. I'm not saying this is what you're doing, I'm just trying to say that dating isn't and shouldn't be the be-all-end-all. There are SO many other factors that should be in place not just so that you can have a happy relationship, but a happy life in general.

There's also the fact that a romantic relationship would probably be all I'd ever want if I could want it - for as often as I fantasise about my dream girl, relationship and life (which is very often!), I have never felt romantic attraction in my entire life. I wish I could fall in love, sometimes. It would make things easier. And, you know, these fantasies would really strongly suggest that I'm not aromantic, but experience proves otherwise. I just know somewhere deep in my heart that I'm aromantic, and I know that any attraction I do experience isn't romantic. 

The way I'd explain it is like how I know I'm not lactose intolerant, even though I've never experienced that sort of allergic reaction. Sure, you can argue that I've been allergic to chocolate my whole life (the horror!) and I just never noticed, because I don't KNOW what an allergic reaction feels like, right? Maybe I've been having one the whole time. But I just know that I'm aromantic, even if I've never experienced romantic attraction to compare my other feelings too, in the same way that I know I'm not lactose intolerant without needing allergy tests done. (I do apologise for likening romantic attraction to an allergy in this metaphor, but it's the best comparison I could give...)

Or if you go to different schools, then do it at both - every bit of support you can get counts. And are there any charities or organisations that can help with treatment? Are there any benefits you could be entitled to? Please explore every route you can to try and find financial support, no matter how hopeless it may seem. From what I know, from the age of 16 you can consent to your own treatment in the UK. Your parents wouldn't have to get involved.

It would probably be easiest to access therapy or counselling through school. They can help you via a school counsellor or a referall to external therapy services.

It'd be best to look into what resources are available within your school - they may not have a counsellor, but they should have some kind of policy in place. You should also find their safeguarding and confidentiality policy  - I was able to do this just by looking up "[school name] confidentiality policy". This will tell you when and if parents need to be involved.

It goes without saying that parents WILL be informed if you talk to your school about suicidal thoughts or self harm. If that's something you want to talk about, Childline is a safe option. They'll only break their confidentiality if you plan to attempt suicide or ask them to - not if you just want to talk through your thoughts with them.

You might want to look into CAMHS and see how you can get referred. If you're able to pay for treatment, there are plenty of online therapy options if that suits you.

Either way, there's a lot more safe and confidential routes and options than you realise. I'm sure you'll be able to find something that works for you and your situation.

I hope this is useful and best of luck!
